Senses.Note: Seven exact witnesses in seven independent works support one Five Ranks relation; the English target follows the conventional relational order while alternates preserve the Chinese pair's older upright/partial vocabulary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正中偏者背理就事。偏中正者舍事入理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Caoshan Yuanzheng (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄): Caoshan Benji explains the relative within the absolute (正中偏) as turning from principle toward affairs and contrasts it with the reverse relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正中偏。霽碧星河冷浸乾。半夜木童敲月戶。暗中驚破玉人眠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Hongzhi (宏智禪師廣錄): Hongzhi Zhengjue's Five Ranks verse presents the rank through a night image of wooden boy, moon door, and jade woman.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是正中偏。汾陽昭云。玉兔既明。初夜後金雞須唱五更前。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mirror of Humans and Devas (人天眼目): a six-rung reviewed unnamed monastic asks about the relative within the absolute (正中偏), and Fenyang Shanzhao answers with moon and cock imagery.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正中偏，三更初夜月明前。莫怪相逢不相識，隱隱猶懷昔日嫌。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianran of Lushan (廬山天然禪師語錄): the headword speaker is an unnamed historical author of the original Five Ranks stanza; the formula “the original verse says” (原頌曰) marks this as an older quoted stanza, but the line, expanded context, section heading, book title, TEI metadata, and available parallel-witness check do not securely name its historical author. Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the relative within the absolute (正中偏) names differentiated appearance within the absolute or upright. Records identify it relationally and then test it through verses, images, and contrast with the absolute within the relative (偏中正). Caoshan Benji explains that the upright position is the empty realm and the partial position the realm of forms; he glosses the relative within the absolute (正中偏) as turning from principle toward affairs and elsewhere as the lord looking toward the minister. Hongzhi Zhengjue's Five Ranks verse gives the rank a night image in which a wooden boy strikes the moon's door and wakes a jade woman. The Mirror of Humans and Devas records an unnamed monastic asking Fenyang Shanzhao for this rank and preserves Fenyang's moon-and-cock response. Langting Ting gives it swallows murmuring between roof beams. Juelang Daosheng relates it to an eastern circle and lesser yang, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies his own shout as this rank once he has mounted the seat. Tianran Hanshi transmits an older night-and-moon verse whose historical author is not established in the available six-rung evidence and then offers his own matching verse, showing that no single image exhausts the relation.
